claim: Visually induced action potentials in the rhesus macaque superior colliculus (SC) occurred intra-saccadically.
source: Despite the ballistic nature of saccades, visually induced action potentials in the rhesus macaque superior colliculus (SC), a structure known to drive eye movements, not only occurred intra-saccadically, but they were also associated with highly predictable modifications of ongoing eye movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing that visual bursts can occur during saccade execution.

claim: Intra-saccadic visually induced action potentials in the SC were associated with highly predictable modifications of ongoing eye movements.
source: Despite the ballistic nature of saccades, visually induced action potentials in the rhesus macaque superior colliculus (SC), a structure known to drive eye movements, not only occurred intra-saccadically, but they were also associated with highly predictable modifications of ongoing eye movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing systematic relationships between intra-saccadic spikes and movement modifications.

claim: Predictable modifications of ongoing eye movements reflected a simultaneity of movement-related discharge at one SC site and visually induced activity at another.
source: Such predictable modifications reflected a simultaneity of movement-related discharge at one SC site and visually induced activity at another.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from simultaneous recordings at different SC sites.

claim: The results suggest instantaneous readout of the SC during movement generation, irrespective of activity source.
source: Our results suggest instantaneous readout of the SC during movement generation, irrespective of activity source, and they explain a significant component of kinematic variability of motor outputs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that movement-unrelated activity affects ongoing movements.

claim: The results explain a significant component of kinematic variability of motor outputs.
source: Our results suggest instantaneous readout of the SC during movement generation, irrespective of activity source, and they explain a significant component of kinematic variability of motor outputs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings relating SC activity to movement variability.

claim: A large fraction of neurons contributing to arm movements are sensory-motor neurons.
source: For example, in different motor modalities like arm (Alexander and Crutcher, 1990; Shen and Alexander, 1997; Breveglieri et al., 2016) or eye (Goldberg and Wurtz, 1972b; Goldberg and Wurtz, 1972a; Wurtz and Goldberg, 1972; Mohler and Wurtz, 1976; Bruce and Goldberg, 1985; Jagadisan and Gandhi, 2019) movements, a large fraction of the neurons contributing to the motor command are also intrinsically sensory in nature, hence being described as sensory-motor neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A large fraction of neurons contributing to eye movements are sensory-motor neurons.
source: For example, in different motor modalities like arm (Alexander and Crutcher, 1990; Shen and Alexander, 1997; Breveglieri et al., 2016) or eye (Goldberg and Wurtz, 1972b; Goldberg and Wurtz, 1972a; Wurtz and Goldberg, 1972; Mohler and Wurtz, 1976; Bruce and Goldberg, 1985; Jagadisan and Gandhi, 2019) movements, a large fraction of the neurons contributing to the motor command are also intrinsically sensory in nature, hence being described as sensory-motor neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The superior colliculus (SC) contains visual-motor neurons.
source: A number of brain areas implicated in eye movement control, such as the midbrain superior colliculus (SC) (Wurtz and Albano, 1980; Munoz and Wurtz, 1995), frontal eye fields (FEF) (Bruce and Goldberg, 1985; Schall and Hanes, 1993; Schall et al., 1995; Tehovnik et al., 2000), and lateral intra-parietal area (LIP) (Mazzoni et al., 1996), contain many so-called visual-motor neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The frontal eye fields (FEF) contain visual-motor neurons.
source: A number of brain areas implicated in eye movement control, such as the midbrain superior colliculus (SC) (Wurtz and Albano, 1980; Munoz and Wurtz, 1995), frontal eye fields (FEF) (Bruce and Goldberg, 1985; Schall and Hanes, 1993; Schall et al., 1995; Tehovnik et al., 2000), and lateral intra-parietal area (LIP) (Mazzoni et al., 1996), contain many so-called visual-motor neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The lateral intra-parietal area (LIP) contains visual-motor neurons.
source: A number of brain areas implicated in eye movement control, such as the midbrain superior colliculus (SC) (Wurtz and Albano, 1980; Munoz and Wurtz, 1995), frontal eye fields (FEF) (Bruce and Goldberg, 1985; Schall and Hanes, 1993; Schall et al., 1995; Tehovnik et al., 2000), and lateral intra-parietal area (LIP) (Mazzoni et al., 1996), contain many so-called visual-motor neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Visual-motor neurons burst both in reaction to visual stimuli entering into their response fields and in association with triggering eye movements towards these response fields.
source: These neurons burst both in reaction to visual stimuli entering into their response fields (RF's) as well as in association with triggering eye movements towards these RF's.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about visual-motor neurons.

claim: In some SC neurons, motor bursts are contingent on the presence of a visual target at the movement endpoint.
source: In some neurons, for example in the SC (Mohler and Wurtz, 1976; Mays and Sparks, 1980; Edelman and Goldberg, 2001; Willeke et al., 2019), even the motor bursts themselves are contingent on the presence of a visual target at the movement endpoint.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Recent proposals suggest that every spike emitted by SC neurons during their motor bursts contributes a mini-vector of movement tendency.
source: In recent proposals (Goossens and Van Opstal, 2006; van Opstal and Goossens, 2008; Goossens and van Opstal, 2012), it was suggested that every spike emitted by SC neurons during their 'motor' bursts contributes a mini-vector of movement tendency, such that the aggregate sum of all output spikes is read out by downstream structures to result in a given movement trajectory.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior models.

claim: Recent SC models assume that only action potentials within a narrow time window around movement triggering matter.
source: However, implicit in these models is the assumption that only action potentials within a narrow time window around movement triggering (the 'motor' burst) matter.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited models.

claim: Recent SC models assume that spiking before or after the eye movement is irrelevant.
source: However, implicit in these models is the assumption that only action potentials within a narrow time window around movement triggering (the 'motor' burst) matter. Any other spiking, by the same or other neurons, before or after the eye movement is irrelevant.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited models.

claim: There is rich behavioral evidence for flexibility to rapidly react to the outside world during late motor control.
source: Indeed, from an ecological perspective, an important reason for multiplexing could be exactly to maintain flexibility to rapidly react to the outside world, even in a late motor control structure, and there is rich behavioral evidence for this (Miles et al., 1986; Gellman et al., 1990; Masson and Perrinet, 2012; Buonocore et al., 2016; Buonocore et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior behavioral research.

claim: The entire landscape of SC activity, not just at the movement burst site, can instantaneously contribute to individual saccade metrics.
source: We found that the entire landscape of SC activity, not just at the movement burst site, can instantaneously contribute to individual saccade metrics, and in a lawful manner, thus explaining a component of behavioral variability previously unaccounted for.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The contribution of movement-unrelated activity to saccade metrics is lawful.
source: We found that the entire landscape of SC activity, not just at the movement burst site, can instantaneously contribute to individual saccade metrics, and in a lawful manner, thus explaining a component of behavioral variability previously unaccounted for.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing systematic relationships.

claim: The detailed properties of movement-unrelated activity contribution depend on the location of the activity on the SC topographic map relative to the movement burst location.
source: Interestingly, the detailed properties of such contribution depend on the location of the movement-unrelated activity on the SC topographic map relative to the movement burst location.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing eccentricity-dependent effects.

claim: Steady-state fixation gives rise to frequent microsaccades.
source: Prior work has shown that this condition gives rise to frequent microsaccades, which are associated with movement-related bursts in the rostral region of the SC representing small visual eccentricities and movement vectors (Hafed et al., 2009; Hafed and Krauzlis, 2012; Chen et al., 2019; Willeke et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Microsaccades are associated with movement-related bursts in the rostral region of the SC.
source: Prior work has shown that this condition gives rise to frequent microsaccades, which are associated with movement-related bursts in the rostral region of the SC representing small visual eccentricities and movement vectors (Hafed et al., 2009; Hafed and Krauzlis, 2012; Chen et al., 2019; Willeke et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In experiment 1, the stimulus consisted of a vertical sine wave grating of 2.2 cycles/deg spatial frequency and variable contrast.
source: For experiment 1, the stimulus consisted of a vertical sine wave grating of 2.2 cycles/deg spatial frequency and variable contrast (Chen et al., 2015; Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: In experiment 2, the stimulus consisted of a high contrast vertical gabor grating of variable spatial frequency and constant contrast.
source: For experiment 2, the stimulus consisted of a high contrast vertical gabor grating of variable spatial frequency and constant contrast (Khademi et al., 2020; Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: All recording sites did not simultaneously burst for microsaccade generation.
source: We ensured that all sites did not simultaneously burst for microsaccade generation (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), to ensure that we were only measuring visual bursts and not concurrent movement-related activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Movement-related activity for microsaccades was in more rostral SC sites, representing foveal visual eccentricities.
source: Such movement-related activity was expectedly in more rostral SC sites, representing foveal visual eccentricities (Chen et al., 2019), as we also explicitly demonstrate in our experiment three described later.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and data from experiment 3.

claim: Across experiments 1 and 2, a total of 128 neurons were measured with RF hotspots indicated in Figure 1C.
source: Across experiments 1 and 2, we measured 'visual' spikes from a total of 128 neurons with RF hotspots indicated by the symbols.
evidence: This is a description of the data collected, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Microsaccades towards the RF were increased in size when they coincided with a peripheral visual burst.
source: Movements towards the RF were increased in size when they coincided with a peripheral visual burst; our subsequent analyses provide a mechanism for this increase.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Microsaccades opposite the RF were slightly truncated.
source: Opposite microsaccades are also shown, and they were slightly truncated.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Across the entire population of neurons from experiments 1 and 2, visual bursts in the SC could occur intra-saccadically.
source: Across the entire population of neurons recorded from both experiments 1 and 2, we found that 'visual' bursts in the SC could occur intra-saccadically.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There were mild but significant modulations of visual burst strength when comparing intra-saccadic and non-saccadic conditions.
source: Statistically, we compared all points in Figure 2C and found mild, but significant, modulations of visual burst strength (t(137) = 2.842, p=0.005).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: SC visual bursts could occur intra-saccadically whether the stimulus was activating the same SC side generating a given movement or the opposite SC side.
source: Moreover, SC visual bursts could still occur intra-saccadically whether the stimulus was activating the same SC side generating a given movement or the opposite SC side (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were modulations in visual burst strength that depended on microsaccade direction relative to the RF location.
source: However, expectedly (Chen et al., 2015), there were modulations in visual burst strength that depended on microsaccade direction relative to the RF location.
evidence: This claim is supported by data and citation to prior research.

claim: There was a transient increase in microsaccade amplitude approximately 80–90 ms after grating onset in experiment 1.
source: As expected (Hafed and Ignashchenkova, 2013; Buonocore et al., 2017; Tian et al., 2018; Malevich et al., 2020b), there was a transient increase in microsaccade amplitude approximately 80–90 ms after grating onset (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and citations to prior research.

claim: The increase in microsaccade amplitude reflected the stimulus properties, being stronger with higher stimulus contrast.
source: Critically, the increase reflected the stimulus properties, because it was stronger with higher stimulus contrast (main effect of contrast: F(2,713) = 81.55, p<1.27427*10−32), and there were also different temporal dynamics: amplitude increases occurred earlier for higher (~75 ms) than lower (~85 ms) contrasts.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Amplitude increases occurred earlier for higher contrast stimuli than for lower contrast stimuli.
source: Critically, the increase reflected the stimulus properties, because it was stronger with higher stimulus contrast (main effect of contrast: F(2,713) = 81.55, p<1.27427*10−32), and there were also different temporal dynamics: amplitude increases occurred earlier for higher (~75 ms) than lower (~85 ms) contrasts.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis.

claim: The alterations in movement metrics were strongly related, in both time and amplitude, with the properties of the SC visual bursts.
source: The alterations in movement metrics in A were strongly related, in both time and amplitude, with the properties of the SC visual bursts.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of data in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The timing of the microsaccadic effects was similar to the timing of the SC visual bursts, showing a short lag of ~20 ms.
source: Moreover, the timing of the microsaccadic effects (Figure 3A) was similar to the timing of the SC visual bursts (Figure 3B), showing a short lag of ~20 ms relative to the bursts that is consistent with an efferent processing delay from SC neurons to the final extraocular muscle drive (Miyashita and Hikosaka, 1996; Jagadisan and Gandhi, 2017; Smalianchuk et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by data comparison and citations to prior research on efferent delays.

claim: The number of extra visual spikes per recorded neuron occurring intra-saccadically was linearly related to metric alterations in microsaccades.
source: The number of extra 'visual' spikes per recorded neuron occurring intra-saccadically was linearly related to metric alterations in microsaccades.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Adding visual spikes into the SC map during ongoing movements systematically increased movement amplitudes.
source: When no spikes were recorded during the eye movement, saccade amplitudes were small (darkest curve). Adding 'visual' spikes into the SC map during the ongoing movements systematically increased movement amplitudes.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was a linear increase in amplitude with each additional spike per recorded neuron for movements towards the RF.
source: There was a linear increase in amplitude with each additional spike per recorded neuron (orange line representing the best linear fit of the underlying raw data).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For movements opposite the RF locations, there was no impact of intra-saccadic visual spikes on movement amplitudes.
source: For movements opposite the RF locations (faint green dots and green line), there was no impact of intra-saccadic 'visual' spikes on movement amplitudes.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Peak radial eye velocities increased for movements towards the RF locations.
source: For the movements towards the RF locations (A), peak radial eye velocities also increased, as expected (Buonocore et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and citation to prior research.

claim: Across all data from experiment 1, the number of visual spikes occurring intra-saccadically was monotonically and linearly driving the amplitude increase of the saccades.
source: Across all data from experiment 1, the number of 'visual' spikes (per recorded neuron) that occurred intra-saccadically was monotonically and linearly driving the amplitude increase of the (smaller) saccades (Figure 4B) (Towards condition, F-statistic vs. constant model: F = 426, p<0.0001; estimated coefficients: intercept = 0.14253, t = 28.989, p<0.0001; slope = 0.066294, t = 20.644, p<0.0001); this relationship also held when we excluded the '0 spike' movements from the analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Microsaccades directed opposite to the RF did not show a similar large positive slope.
source: On the other hand, microsaccades directed opposite to the RF (Figure 4B) did not show a similar large positive slope; and a trend for a negative slope was not statistically significant (Opposite condition, F-statistic vs. constant model: F = 2.22, p=0.137; estimated coefficients: intercept = 0.1185, t = 56.261, p<0.0001; slope = −0.0028872, t = −1.488, p=0.137).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Every SC spike matters: all activity happening intra-saccadically and at locations of the SC map different from the saccade endpoint goal is interpreted as part of the motor command by downstream neurons.
source: These results suggest that there is an instantaneous specification of saccade metrics described by the overall activity present on the SC map, and they provide a much more nuanced view of the correlations between SC visual bursts and microsaccade amplitudes shown in Figures 2B and 3. Every SC spike matters: all activity happening intra-saccadically and at locations of the SC map different from the saccade endpoint goal is interpreted as part of the motor command by downstream neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Visual spiking activity in even purely visual neurons was still positively correlated with increased microsaccade amplitudes.
source: Most interestingly, visual spiking activity in even purely visual neurons was still positively correlated with increased microsaccade amplitudes, although the effect was weaker than that of visual spiking activity in the deeper visual-motor neurons of the SC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The distance of the extra spiking activity on the SC map from the planned movement vector matters.
source: The effects were still present but with a notably smaller slope than in Figure 4, suggesting that the distance of the 'extra' spiking activity on the SC map from the planned movement vector matters (Towards condition, F-statistic vs. constant model: F = 45.1, p<2.03*10−11; estimated coefficients: intercept = 0.12368, t = 57.252, p<0.0001; slope = 0.0098876, t = 6.7195, p<2.024*10−11).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing near and far neurons.

claim: There was a significant interaction between eccentricity and the number of injected spikes.
source: We added eccentricity to our generalized linear model analysis, and there was a significant interaction between eccentricity and the number of injected spikes (slope = −0.0080709, t = −14.585, p<0.0001): the slope of the relationship between the number of 'injected' visual spikes and microsaccade amplitude decreased as a function of increasing eccentricity.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: For eccentricities larger than approximately 4–5 deg, there was a weaker impact of additional injected visual spikes on microsaccade amplitudes than for smaller eccentricities.
source: For eccentricities larger than approximately 4–5 deg, there was a weaker impact of additional 'injected' visual spikes on microsaccade amplitudes than for smaller eccentricities (which justifies our choice in other figures to focus on neurons with preferred eccentricities ≤ 4.5 deg).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The slope of the relationship between injected visual spikes and microsaccade amplitude always remained positive across all tested eccentricities.
source: However, and most critically, the slope always remained positive. This means that there was never a negative impact of 'injected' visual spikes on microsaccade amplitudes. The readout always involved 'adding' to the movement amplitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Whenever SC visual bursts occurred pre- and intra-saccadically, microsaccade amplitudes were dramatically increased by two- to three-fold relative to baseline microsaccade amplitudes.
source: As can be seen, whenever SC 'visual' bursts occurred pre- and intra-saccadically, microsaccade amplitudes were dramatically increased by two- to three-fold relative to baseline microsaccade amplitudes (blue horizontal lines).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: For visual bursts after peak velocity, the effect on microsaccade amplitude was diminished.
source: For visual bursts after peak velocity (Figure 5C), the effect was diminished, consistent with efferent delays from SC activity to extraocular muscle activation (Miyashita and Hikosaka, 1996; Munoz et al., 1996; Stanford et al., 1996; Gandhi and Keller, 1999b; Katnani and Gandhi, 2012; Jagadisan and Gandhi, 2017; Smalianchuk et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and citations to prior research.

claim: At the time at which SC activity is to be read out by downstream neurons to implement a saccadic eye movement, additional movement-unrelated SC spiking activity is also read out and has a direct impact on eye movement metrics.
source: Therefore, our results so far suggest that at the time at which SC activity is to be read out by downstream neurons to implement a saccadic eye movement (right before movement onset to right before movement end, e.g. Miyashita and Hikosaka, 1996; Munoz et al., 1996; Stanford et al., 1996; Gandhi and Keller, 1999b; Katnani and Gandhi, 2012; Jagadisan and Gandhi, 2017; Smalianchuk et al., 2018), additional movement-unrelated SC spiking activity is also read out and has a direct impact on eye movement metrics.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and citations to prior research.

claim: The larger movements were always associated with the presence of extra visual spikes on the SC map occurring between −30 ms and +30 ms from saccade onset.
source: For all other amplitude bins, the larger movements were always associated with the presence of extra 'visual' spikes on the SC map (more eccentric than the normal microsaccade amplitudes) occurring between −30 ms and +30 ms from saccade onset (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The timing of the effect was constant across amplitude bins, suggesting that it was the relative timing of extra visual spikes and movement onset that mattered.
source: Note how the timing of the effect was constant across amplitude bins, suggesting that it was the relative timing of extra 'visual' spikes and movement onset that mattered; the amplitude effect (that is, the different colored curves) simply reflected the total number of spikes that occurred during the critical time window of movement triggering.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Additional visual spikes in the SC at a time consistent with saccade-related readout by downstream neurons essentially leak into the saccade being generated.
source: Therefore, additional 'visual' spikes in the SC at a time consistent with saccade-related readout by downstream neurons essentially 'leak' into the saccade being generated.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: For movements going opposite to the recorded neuron's RFs, there was a lower number of spikes happening during the peri-saccadic interval.
source: On the other hand, the pattern of Figure 6A was not present for movements going opposite to the recorded neuron's RF's, for which, if anything, there was a lower number of spikes happening during the peri-saccadic interval (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: It was easier to trigger microsaccades in one direction when no activity was present in the opposite SC.
source: This suggests that it was easier to trigger microsaccades in one direction when no activity was present in the opposite SC.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Once a movement-unrelated spike is properly temporally aligned with the motor burst, it can still have a similar behavioral impact on movement amplitudes whether the spike was far or near in eccentricity.
source: This is an important finding because it suggests that once a movement-unrelated spike is properly temporally aligned with the motor burst, it can still have a similar behavioral impact on movement amplitudes whether the spike was far or near in eccentricity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The global reduction of behavioral effects with more eccentric stimuli could reflect a reduced likelihood of temporal alignment between the visual spikes and the population of neurons bursting as part of the movement command.
source: This suggests that the global reduction of behavioral effects that we saw with more eccentric stimuli (e.g. Figure 3—figure supplement 1) could reflect a reduced likelihood of temporal alignment between the 'visual' spikes and the population of neurons bursting as part of the movement command.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: After the initial visual bursts had subsided, SC neurons maintained a lower level of sustained discharge for a prolonged period of time in experiment 2.
source: This meant that after the initial visual bursts had subsided, SC neurons maintained a lower level of 'sustained' discharge for a prolonged period of time, a discharge that was often absent in the absence of stimuli since some SC neurons do not exhibit any baseline discharge.
evidence: This is a description of the observed neural activity in experiment 2.

claim: For the example neuron in Figure 7A, towards movements were increased in amplitude with every injected extra spike from the sustained discharge of the recorded neuron.
source: The 'towards movements' were increased in amplitude with every injected extra spike from the 'sustained' discharge of the recorded neuron (F-statistic vs. constant model: F = 383, p=0.0325; estimated coefficients: intercept = 0.1105, t = 17.67, p=0.0360; slope = 0.0948, t = 19.57, p=0.0324), whereas opposite movements were not (F-statistic vs. constant model: F = 6.15, p=0.2440; estimated coefficients: intercept = 0.1348, t = 24.49, p=0.0250; slope = −0.0101, t = −2.47, p=0.2440).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Across all neurons collected from experiment 2, there were robust effects of individual neuronal spiking and microsaccade amplitudes for sustained discharge.
source: Across all neurons collected from experiment 2, in which we had the opportunity to look for spiking outside of the 'burst' intervals due to the longer trial durations, we found robust effects of individual neuronal spiking and microsaccade amplitudes (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: For movements towards the RF, every additional sustained spike linearly increased microsaccade amplitude with a slope of 0.0126 deg/spike.
source: For movements towards the RF, every additional 'sustained' spike linearly increased microsaccade amplitude with a slope of 0.0126 deg/spike (F-statistic vs. constant model: F = 13.1, p=0.0364; estimated coefficients: intercept = 0.1098, t = 12.87, p=0.0010; slope = 0.0126, t = 3.61, p=0.0363).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The impact of each spike during sustained discharge was smaller in magnitude than the impact of each spike during burst discharge.
source: Of course, quantitatively, the impact of each spike in Figure 7D (for 'towards' movements) was smaller in magnitude than the impact of each spike in Figure 4B (for similar 'towards' movements).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of data in Figure 7D and Figure 4B.

claim: During visual bursts, a large population of SC neurons are expected to be bursting simultaneously.
source: However, this is fully expected: during the visual bursts, a large population of SC neurons are expected to be bursting simultaneously (Lee et al., 1988); on the other hand, during 'sustained' discharge, different individual neurons may or may not be simultaneously active depending on a variety of factors related to their individual spatio-temporal RF properties (Churan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on citations to prior research and inference.

claim: There is a tight time window around saccade onset in which any movement-unrelated spikes in sites other than the saccade goal representation can induce a systematic variation in the motor program.
source: To summarize the overall results so far, we found that there is a tight time window around saccade onset (Figures 5–7) in which any movement-unrelated spikes in sites other than the saccade goal representation can induce a systematic variation in the motor program.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Movement-related firing rate for all rostral SC neurons was observed when microsaccades towards the movement RF occurred 30–100 ms after peripheral stimulus onset.
source: Left panel: movement-related firing rate for all rostral SC neurons when microsaccades towards the movement RF occurred 30–100 ms after peripheral stimulus onset (i.e. coincident with peripheral visual burst occurrence).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11A.

claim: The rostral SC clearly exhibited bursts at the same time as peripheral visual bursts when microsaccades occurred.
source: Right panel: When the same data were aligned to stimulus onset (as opposed to microsaccade onset), we could see that the rostral SC clearly exhibited bursts at the same time as peripheral visual bursts when microsaccades occurred (red).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11A.

claim: When microsaccades did not occur, peripheral stimulus onsets in either direction suppressed rostral SC activity.
source: When microsaccades did not occur, peripheral stimulus onsets in either direction suppressed rostral SC activity (blue curves).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11A.

claim: Peripheral visual bursts still occurred even when coincident microsaccades occurred.
source: Consistent with all of our earlier results, peripheral visual bursts still occurred even when coincident microsaccades occurred (red).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11B.

claim: There was no significant alteration of the rostral motor bursts by the presence of a peripheral visual burst across the population.
source: Across the population, there was no significant alteration of the rostral motor bursts by the presence of a peripheral visual burst (Figure 12A; p=0.12539, paired ranksum test, N = 42 neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 12A.

claim: Microsaccade amplitudes were significantly larger for the movements coincident with the peripheral visual bursts compared to baseline.
source: Microsaccade amplitudes were significantly larger for the movements coincident with the peripheral visual bursts (p=7.9073×10−27; t-test; N = 650 microsaccades with peripheral stimulus onset, and N = 1956 baseline microsaccades).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 12B.

claim: The results reveal a component of motor variability that has been previously unaccounted for.
source: Our results reveal a component of motor variability that we believe has been previously unaccounted for, namely, the fact that ever-present spiking activity in the entire SC map (whether due to sustained firing rates for a stimulus presented in the RF, like in Figure 7, or otherwise) can 'leak' into the readout performed by downstream motor structures when executing a movement.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Saccades during natural viewing show an immense amount of kinematic variability when compared to simplified laboratory tasks with only a single saccade target.
source: Indeed, saccades during natural viewing show an immense amount of kinematic variability when compared to simplified laboratory tasks with only a single saccade target (Berg et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The results demonstrate a remarkable flexibility of the oculomotor system during eye movement generation.
source: From an ecological perspective, our results demonstrate a remarkable flexibility of the oculomotor system during eye movement generation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Saccades were thought to be controlled by an open-loop control system due to their apparent ballistic nature.
source: Historically, saccades were thought to be controlled by an open-loop control system due to their apparent ballistic nature.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about historical views of saccade control.

claim: Individual saccades are actually malleable brain processes.
source: However, other evidence, including our current results, clearly showed that individual saccades are actually malleable brain processes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the current results and other evidence.

claim: Dual-site suprathreshold simultaneous SC microstimulation results in saccades to neither burst location.
source: In the laboratory, this extra activity can also be completely artificial, as is the case with electrical microstimulation (Katnani and Gandhi, 2011; Katnani et al., 2012); for example, dual-site suprathreshold simultaneous SC microstimulation results in saccades to neither 'burst' location, consistent with the deviations that we observed for our microsaccades.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The integration of sensory signals into the motor plan exhibited a lawful additive process between the visual spikes injected into the SC population and the altered microsaccade amplitudes.
source: The integration that we observed of sensory signals into the motor plan was not merely a 'loose' leakage phenomenon; rather, it exhibited a lawful additive process between the 'visual' spikes injected into the SC population and the altered microsaccade amplitudes (Figures 4–7).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The more visual spikes that occurred intra-saccadically, the larger the microsaccades became, following a linear relationship.
source: The more 'visual' spikes that occurred intra-saccadically, the larger the microsaccades became, following a linear relationship.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: This additive mechanism might underlie many of the effects commonly seen in experimental psychophysics, in which saccade kinematics are systematically altered by the presence of sudden irrelevant visual information.
source: We suggest that this additive mechanism might underlie many of the effects commonly seen in experimental psychophysics, in which saccade kinematics are systematically altered by the presence of sudden irrelevant visual information available as close as 40 ms to movement onset (Edelman and Xu, 2009; Buonocore and McIntosh, 2012; Guillaume, 2012; Buonocore et al., 2016; Buonocore et al., 2017; Malevich et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is based on speculation and citations to prior research.

claim: These modulations are a behavioral manifestation of the instantaneous readout of the activity on the SC map.
source: Our hypothesis is that these modulations are a behavioral manifestation of the instantaneous readout of the activity on the SC map, as we also previously hypothesized (Hafed and Ignashchenkova, 2013; Buonocore et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on speculation and citations to prior hypotheses.

claim: Similar specification mechanisms can be seen in the instantaneous alteration of eye velocity during smooth pursuit when small flashes are presented.
source: Moreover, similar specification mechanisms can be seen in the instantaneous alteration of eye velocity during smooth pursuit when small flashes are presented (Buonocore et al., 2019), and even with ocular position drift during fixation (Malevich et al., 2020a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The observations extend the mechanisms uncovered in this study to the pursuit system and beyond.
source: These observations extend the mechanisms uncovered in our study to the pursuit system and beyond, and they also relate to sequential activation of SC neurons during curved saccades associated with planning sequences of movements (Port and Wurtz, 2003).
evidence: This claim is based on inference and citation to prior research.

claim: The observations are consistent with experimental manipulations in which the oculomotor gate in the brainstem is opened by blinks.
source: These observations are also consistent with experimental manipulations in which the oculomotor 'gate' in the brainstem is 'opened' by blinks (Jagadisan and Gandhi, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Blinks during saccade planning revealed that preparatory spikes in the SC before saccade onset contain a kind of movement potential.
source: In such manipulations, the authors exploited the fact that blinks are associated with pauses in brainstem omnipause neuron activity, and they revealed that blinks during saccade planning revealed that preparatory spikes in the SC before saccade onset contain a kind of 'movement potential' (Jagadisan and Gandhi, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The investigations provide a means to precisely quantify behavioral modulations when sensory stimuli arrive in close temporal proximity to saccade generation.
source: Our investigations, which were driven by behavioral modulations observed in psychophysical experiments as alluded to above, therefore now provide a means to precisely quantify such behavioral modulations when sensory stimuli arrive in close temporal proximity to saccade generation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: The sensory burst may act as a motor program itself, as with express saccades having ultra-short latencies that appear to merge SC visual and motor bursts.
source: In that sense, the sensory burst may act as a motor program itself, as with express saccades having ultra-short latencies that appear to merge SC visual and motor bursts (Edelman and Keller, 1996; Sparks et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is based on speculation and citations to prior research.

claim: The results motivate similar neurophysiological studies on sensory-motor integration in other oculomotor structures.
source: Most intriguingly, our results motivate similar neurophysiological studies on sensory-motor integration in other oculomotor structures.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about future research directions.

claim: Ongoing experiments in the lower oculomotor brainstem are revealing highly thought provoking visual pattern analysis capabilities of intrinsically motor neurons.
source: For example, our own ongoing experiments in the lower oculomotor brainstem, at the very final stage for saccade control (Keller, 1974; Büttner-Ennever et al., 1988; Gandhi and Keller, 1999a; Missal and Keller, 2002), are revealing highly thought provoking visual pattern analysis capabilities of intrinsically motor neurons (Buonocore et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to ongoing work.

claim: The results are consistent with the mini-vector model in the sense that linear contributions of additional SC spikes on eye movement metrics were observed.
source: Our results are consistent with this model, and related ones also invoking a role of SC activity levels in instantaneous trajectory control (Waitzman et al., 1991; Smalianchuk et al., 2018), in the sense that we did observe linear contributions of additional SC spikes on eye movement metrics (Figures 4, 6 and 7).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and citations to prior models.

claim: The results add to the mini-vector model the notion that there need not be a classifier identifying particular SC spikes as being the movement-related spikes of the current movement and other spikes as being irrelevant.
source: However, our results add to this model the notion that there need not be a 'classifier' identifying particular SC spikes as being the movement-related spikes of the current movement and other spikes as being irrelevant.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Diminishing returns of relative eccentricity between the extra spikes and the current motor burst were found.
source: More importantly, we found diminishing returns of relative eccentricity between the 'extra' spikes and the current motor burst (e.g. Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The mini-vector model needs to consider local and remote interactions more explicitly.
source: Therefore, this model needs to consider local and remote interactions more explicitly.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: The SC generates fewer saccade-related spikes during FEF inactivation, even for matched saccade amplitudes.
source: Indeed, Peel et al., 2020 reported that the SC generates fewer saccade-related spikes during FEF inactivation, even for matched saccade amplitudes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The link between SC motor burst spiking and saccade kinematics is more loose than suggested by the mini-vector model.
source: Thus, the link between SC motor burst spiking and saccade kinematics is more loose than suggested by the model.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited research.

claim: Microsaccades without visual guidance can be associated with substantially fewer active SC neurons than similarly-sized microsaccades with visual guidance.
source: Similarly, we recently found that microsaccades without visual guidance can be associated with substantially fewer active SC neurons than similarly-sized microsaccades with visual guidance, because of so-called visually-dependent saccade-related neurons (Willeke et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: SC motor bursts are different for saccades directed to upper versus lower visual field locations.
source: Finally, SC motor bursts themselves are different for saccades directed to upper versus lower visual field locations (Hafed and Chen, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Further research on the functional roles of SC motor bursts is strongly needed.
source: All these observations suggest that further research on the functional roles of SC motor bursts is strongly needed.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the discussed observations.

claim: Dual-site SC microstimulation supports vector averaging models.
source: Indeed, dual-site SC microstimulation (Katnani et al., 2012) supports vector averaging models, and it is also conceptually similar to our approach.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In its purest form, vector averaging still cannot account for the behavioral observations with far stimuli and neurons.
source: However, in its purest form, vector averaging still cannot account for our behavioral observations with far stimuli and neurons (e.g, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Jagadisan and Gandhi suggested that saccades are not triggered except if there was substantial population temporal alignment among active neurons.
source: In recent work, Jagadisan and Gandhi, 2019 suggested that saccades are not triggered except if there was substantial population temporal alignment among active neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Motor bursts have stronger temporal alignment between active neurons than visual bursts.
source: They found that motor bursts have stronger temporal alignment between active neurons than visual bursts.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The idea of temporal alignment provides a plausible explanation for why the strongest impact of visual spikes on movement metrics was found in a very specific time window around movement onset.
source: This idea is appealing to us because it provides a plausible explanation for why we found the strongest impact of 'visual' spikes on movement metrics in a very specific time window around movement onset (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and cited ideas.

claim: The weaker behavioral effects with increasing eccentricity could be explained by more variable visual bursts of far neurons reducing the likelihood of temporal alignment.
source: In our view, this idea can also account for our weaker behavioral effects with increasing eccentricity. Specifically, because peripheral SC neurons prefer lower spatial frequencies than central SC neurons (Chen et al., 2018), the visual bursts of far neurons (for similar stimuli) could be more variable than the bursts of near neurons. This decreases the likelihood of temporal alignment in Figure 6, and therefore reduces the behavioral impact of the peripheral spikes.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation and citations to prior research.

claim: Peripheral visual bursts may be associated with reductions in rostral SC activity.
source: On the one hand, we confirmed that peripheral visual bursts may be associated with reductions in rostral SC activity, as we and others had also previously observed (Munoz and Istvan, 1998; Hafed and Krauzlis, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior research.

claim: Rostral SC inhibition only occurred in the complete absence of microsaccades.
source: However, rostral SC inhibition only occurred in the complete absence of microsaccades (Figures 9–12).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 9–12.

claim: When microsaccades were triggered simultaneously with peripheral visual bursts, the rostral SC neurons actually exhibited activity bursts.
source: On the contrary, when microsaccades were triggered simultaneously with peripheral visual bursts, the rostral SC neurons actually exhibited activity bursts (Figures 9–12).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 9–12.

claim: Lateral interactions do not necessarily mean that a visual burst at one SC map location automatically implies a pausing of activity at distant locations.
source: Therefore, lateral interactions do not necessarily mean that a visual burst at one SC map location automatically implies a pausing of activity at distant locations.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Bursts happen in both the rostral and caudal SC, with the caudal bursts kinematically adding to the generated saccades.
source: Rather, bursts happen in both the rostral and caudal SC, with the caudal 'bursts' kinematically adding to the generated saccades.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The analyses in Figures 4 and 7 are analogous to choice probability analyses in other fields.
source: Finally, our analyses in Figures 4 and 7 are analogous to 'choice probability' analyses in other fields (Britten et al., 1996; Nienborg and Cumming, 2006).
evidence: This claim is based on inference and citations to prior research.

claim: Individual injected spikes in the SC correlated remarkably well with saccade metric changes.
source: In our case, we found that individual 'injected' spikes in the SC correlated remarkably well with saccade metric changes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The impact of a single extra visual spike from a visual-motor neuron was stronger than that of a single extra spike from a visual neuron.
source: However, the impact of a single extra visual spike from a visual-motor neuron was stronger than that of a single extra spike from a visual neuron.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Visual-motor neurons are the SC output neurons.
source: This is consistent with suggestions that visual-motor neurons are the SC output neurons (Mohler and Wurtz, 1976), and it is also consistent with our earlier observations that under specific conditions, visual-motor neurons are what might dictate saccadic behavior (Chen and Hafed, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The results expose highly plausible neural mechanisms associated with robust behavioral effects on saccades accompanied by nearby visual flashes in a variety of paradigms.
source: Our results expose highly plausible neural mechanisms associated with robust behavioral effects on saccades accompanied by nearby visual flashes in a variety of paradigms, and they also motivate revisiting a classic neurophysiological problem, the role of the SC in saccade control, from the perspective of visual-motor multiplexing within individual brain circuits, and even individual neurons themselves.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Data were collected from two adult, male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) that were 6–8 years of age and weighed 6–8 kg.
source: We collected data from two adult, male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) that were 6–8 years of age and weighed 6–8 kg.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: The experiments were approved by ethics committees at the regional governmental offices of the city of Tuebingen.
source: The experiments were approved (licenses: CIN3/13; CIN4/19G) by ethics committees at the regional governmental offices of the city of Tuebingen and were in accordance with European Union guidelines on animal research and the associated implementations of these guidelines in German law.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Eye movements were recorded with high temporal and spatial precision using a scleral search coil.
source: To record eye movements with high temporal and spatial precision, the monkeys were also implanted with a scleral search coil. This allowed eye tracking using the magnetic induction technique (Fuchs and Robinson, 1966; Judge et al., 1980).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: A total of 84 SC visual and visual-motor neurons were analyzed in experiment 1.
source: Overall, we analyzed 84 SC visual (44) and visual-motor (40) neurons in two monkeys.
evidence: This is a description of the data collected.

claim: A total of 55 neurons were analyzed in experiment 2.
source: We analyzed the activity of 55 neurons from this task (31 visual and 24 visual motor); 11 of these neurons were also tested with the contrast task described above within the same sessions.
evidence: This is a description of the data collected.

claim: A total of 42 rostral SC neurons and 54 caudal SC neurons were isolated for analysis in experiment 3.
source: Across all sessions, we isolated offline (see below) 42 rostral SC neurons and 54 caudal SC neurons for further analysis in the current study.
evidence: This is a description of the data collected.
